exam: A 5‑year‑old with sickle cell presents with fever and a painful leg swelling – which immune barrier failure is most likely and what is your immediate management? — Recognise skin breach with possible cellulitis; start empiric antibiotics, obtain wound culture, assess for osteomyelitis.

A patient on ART with CD4 150 develops chronic cough and weight loss – which diagnostic test answers the key question and why? — Order sputum GeneXpert for TB; low CD4 predisposes to reactivation, and GeneXpert gives rapid detection.

In a malaria‑endemic clinic, a child has fever, pallor and jaundice but no malaria test is available – what bedside investigation helps you decide if haemolysis is immune‑mediated? — Perform a direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test if possible; if unavailable, look for dark urine and reticulocytosis to support immune haemolysis.

A trauma patient arrives with a large contaminated laceration; what is the first step to restore barrier function? — Perform thorough irrigation and debridement; this removes bacterial load and re‑establishes the physical barrier.
Why is complement measurement rarely useful in acute sepsis in low‑resource settings? — Results are delayed and do not change immediate management; focus on clinical assessment and early antibiotics.

A pregnant woman in a rural hospital develops a rash and fever; you suspect varicella – which immune mechanism is compromised and what prophylaxis is indicated? — Cell‑mediated immunity is key; give acyclovir if within 24 h and vaccinate contacts if non‑immune.

Explain why steroids are contraindicated in a patient with uncontrolled bacterial cellulitis. — Steroids suppress neutrophil function and cytokine response, worsening the innate defence needed to contain the infection.

A child with severe malnutrition presents with recurrent infections – which barrier is most affected and how can you support it? — Physical barrier (skin and mucosa) is thinned; provide nutritional rehabilitation, zinc supplementation, and protect skin from trauma.
ai.title: Immune System Protective Mechanisms
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: The immune system defends the host through layered barriers, innate cells and soluble factors, and adaptive responses. Clinicians must recognise how each layer fails in common tropical infections and how limited resources affect assessment.

b: Physical barrier: skin, mucosa, tight junctions
Chemical barrier: lysozyme, acidic pH, antimicrobial peptides
Biological barrier: normal flora competing with pathogens
Cellular innate: neutrophils, macrophages, dendritic cells, NK cells
Humoral innate: complement, acute‑phase proteins, interferons
Adaptive: B‑cell antibodies, T‑cell mediated immunity
sections.p: Protection begins at epithelial surfaces, continues with cellular and soluble innate components, and culminates in antigen‑specific adaptive immunity. Understanding the hierarchy helps pinpoint where disease breaches occur.

b: Skin breach: Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes
Mucosal breach: Neisseria meningitidis, Candida spp.
Intracellular invasion: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, HIV
sections.p: Pathogens exploit specific weaknesses in each defence layer – e.g., HIV depletes CD4+ T cells, malaria parasites invade red cells, and helminths secrete proteases that disrupt mucosal tight junctions.

b: Respiratory: TB, influenza – cross damaged mucosa
Water‑borne: Vibrio cholerae – acid‑labile, needs high inoculum
Vector‑borne: Plasmodium – skin puncture bypasses epidermis
sections.p: Most infections reach the host via respiratory droplets, contaminated water, insect vectors, or percutaneous injury, then must overcome the barrier hierarchy to establish disease.

b: Skin breach → cellulitis, necrotising fasciitis
Mucosal breach → pneumonia, meningitis
Cellular immunity loss → disseminated TB, cryptococcal meningitis
sections.p: When barriers fail, clinical syndromes arise that reflect the level of breach – from superficial cellulitis to systemic sepsis or opportunistic infections in immunocompromised patients.

t.b: Is there a visible breach or ulcer? Guides need for wound cultures and empiric coverage
Leukocytosis or neutropenia? Indicates innate response status; if unavailable, use bedside white cell count (manual) or clinical signs of infection
Quantifies adaptive immunity; <200 cells/µL predicts opportunistic infections
Low complement suggests hereditary deficiency or consumption in severe bacterial sepsis
Detects Plasmodium antigens; a positive result explains fever despite intact barriers

b: Wound care: debridement, sterile dressings – restores physical barrier
Broad‑spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ampicillin‑sulbactam) for cellulitis – covers common skin flora
Antiretroviral therapy for HIV – preserves CD4 cells
Vaccination (e.g., pneumococcal, Hib) – primes adaptive immunity
Nutritional support (protein, zinc) – enhances barrier and cellular immunity
sections.p: Management starts with restoring barrier integrity, then targeting the offending pathogen, and finally supporting innate and adaptive functions.

b: Identify which barrier is breached based on presentation
Choose the most appropriate bedside test when laboratory facilities are limited
Explain why steroids are avoided in uncontrolled bacterial infection
sections.p: Exam questions often link a clinical scenario to the specific defence that failed and ask for the next investigative or therapeutic step.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly expanding cellulitis with systemic toxicity
Severe sepsis signs (hypotension, altered mental status)
New onset fever in an HIV patient with CD4 <200
